llm.summary: The skill's files and instructions are largely coherent with an SDK for running OpenServ agents, but there are notable concerns (prompt‑injection indicators, automated writing of a wallet private key to .env, and automatic tunnel to a proxy) that merit careful review before installation.

dimensions.detail: The name/description match the included SKILL.md and example code: this is an SDK for building OpenServ agents. The examples and reference describe agent provisioning, runless/runnable capabilities, task/file APIs, payments, and web3 registration — all consistent with an agent SDK. The required env/credentials declared as 'none' aligns with the skill promoting platform-delegated LLM calls and provision() to create agent credentials.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs the developer to call provision(), which will create a wallet and write WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY (and agent API keys/tokens) into .env at runtime and to reload dotenv. That is expected for this platform but is sensitive: it instructs writing a private key to disk and programmatic reloading of env. The docs also direct use of an automatic tunnel (agents-proxy.openserv.ai) and give shell commands (e.g., lsof | xargs kill -9). There is also a pre-scan flag for 'system-prompt-override' which suggests prompt-injection patterns were detected in the SKILL.md; this should be examined further because instruction text could be used to manipulate agent/system prompts or other runtime policy.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec (instruction-only skill with example code). That lowers install-time risk because nothing is downloaded or executed automatically by an installer. Example files are plain TypeScript examples and docs — no third-party binary downloads are embedded in the skill bundle.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required environment variables, but the docs explain that provision() will create and write WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY, OPENSERV_API_KEY, and OPENSERV_AUTH_TOKEN to .env. Asking to persist a wallet private key to disk is sensitive but coherent with the described web3/registration functionality. The skill also mentions optional OPENAI_API_KEY only when using direct OpenAI calls. No unrelated credentials are requested, but writing private keys to .env increases attack surface and operational risk.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill's recommended workflow instructs provision() to generate credentials and persist WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY and agent tokens to .env at runtime. While creating and storing agent-specific credentials is expected for this SDK, it is persistent storage of a highly sensitive secret. The skill does not request 'always: true' and does not modify other skills, but the automatic tunnel (agents-proxy.openserv.ai) and written private key are persistence/privilege considerations that deserve caution.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This package appears to be a genuine SDK for running OpenServ agents, but take these precautions before installing or running it: 1) Verify the source: the registry metadata shows 'unknown' source and no homepage — confirm the package origin (npm/GitHub/org) and inspect the actual @openserv-labs/client and sdk packages before running. 2) Review provision() behavior in the client package: it will create a wallet and write WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY to .env; consider using an ephemeral/funded test wallet and do not reuse keys from important accounts. 3) Avoid storing high-value private keys on production machines or in repositories; if you must persist keys, use a secure secret store rather than plaintext .env. 4) Be aware run() opens an automatic tunnel to agents-proxy.openserv.ai and the SDK documents contacting api.openserv.ai — audit network flows and firewall policy as needed. 5) The pre-scan flagged potential prompt-injection patterns in SKILL.md; read the full SKILL.md and examples for any instructions that tell code or agents to ignore other policies or to override system prompts, and do not deploy code that suppresses security controls. 6) If you plan to use direct LLM providers (process()), avoid putting provider API keys into the same workspace env unless necessary; prefer platform-delegated generate() where possible. 7) If unsure, run the examples in an isolated/dev environment with limited privileges and funds and inspect the behavior of provision()/PlatformClient before trusting it with real credentials.
llm.findings: [system-prompt-override] unexpected: The SKILL.md was flagged for 'system-prompt-override' patterns by the pre-scan. The skill is an SDK and naturally discusses system prompts and agent prompts, but any pattern that looks like an attempt to override or manipulate system-level prompts should be inspected. This could be benign documentation text, but it's worth verifying that the content does not include instructions intended to subvert evaluation or runtime policies.
